title: Local and constant factors of a finite commutative group scheme over an algebraically closed field
statement: Let $K$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure], and let $G$ be a finite commutative $K$-group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme]. Let $C$ be the connected component containing the identity, with its open-and-closed subscheme structure (connected means not a disjoint union of two nonempty open subsets). Then $C$ is a finite connected commutative subgroup scheme. The group $H=G(K)$ is finite. Write $H_K=\coprod_{h\in H}\operatorname{Spec}K$ for the constant group scheme, with addition induced by that of $H$. The morphism $C\times_K H_K\to G$ whose restriction to the component indexed by $h$ is translation by $h$ is an isomorphism of group schemes. The coordinate algebra $B=\Gamma(C,\mathcal O_C)$ is a nonzero finite-dimensional commutative local $K$-algebra: it has exactly one maximal ideal $I$, and $I=\ker(\epsilon:B\to K)$ for evaluation $\epsilon$ at the identity, so its residue field is $K$. In particular, putting $d=\dim_K B$ and $q=|H|$, one has $d,q\geq1$ and $\dim_K\Gamma(G,\mathcal O_G)=dq$.

source.place: Proposition 11.3, printed p.210 (split connected-etale sequence over a perfect field), Proposition 2.37, printed pp.51-52, and Propositions 11.1-11.2, printed pp.209-210 (local Artinian components); commutative case over an algebraically closed field.

proof.text: Put $A=\Gamma(G,\mathcal O_G)$. By [lem-weil-pbc-finite-over-field-affine-finite-dim], $G=\operatorname{Spec}A$ over $K$ and $A$ is finite-dimensional. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-finite-over-zero-dim-local-discrete-spectrum] with $R=K$ and maximal ideal $(0)$: $|G|$ is finite discrete. For each point $x$, let $U_x$ be its one-point open subscheme; these are disjoint, clopen and cover $G$. By [lem-weil-pbc-finite-discrete-scheme-affine], $U_x=\operatorname{Spec}B_x$, where $B_x=\Gamma(U_x,\mathcal O_G)$. The sheaf gluing axiom on this disjoint finite cover gives $A\simeq\prod_x B_x$ as $K$-algebras. Thus every $B_x$ is finite-dimensional (projection is surjective), nonzero, and local: its spectrum has exactly one prime, hence exactly one maximal ideal. It is Artinian by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-dim-algebra-artinian]. In particular $U_x\to\operatorname{Spec}K$ is finite, by the affine definition of finiteness.

source.place: Propositions 11.1–11.3, printed pp.209–210; direct componentwise expansion over an algebraically closed field

proof.text: For every $x$, [lem-sc-finite-nonempty-point] applies to the nonempty finite $K$-scheme $U_x$ and supplies a $K$-point, equivalently a $K$-algebra homomorphism $\epsilon_x:B_x\to K$ by [def-weil-affine-spectrum]. This homomorphism is surjective since it fixes $K$, and its kernel is the unique maximal ideal $\mathfrak m_x$. Hence $B_x/\mathfrak m_x\simeq K$ as $K$-algebras. By [lem-weil-pbc-artinian-local-noetherian-nilpotent], $\mathfrak m_x$ is nilpotent. Every $K$-algebra homomorphism $B_x\to K$ kills this ideal, since a field has no nonzero nilpotents; on the quotient $K$ it must be the identity. Thus $U_x$ has exactly one $K$-point. A $K$-point of $G$ factors uniquely through the open containing its image, so $H=G(K)$ is in bijection with the finite set $|G|$. It is a commutative group under the group-scheme operations, with identity $0$. The component $C=U_0$ has coordinate algebra $B=B_0$, unique maximal ideal $I=\ker\epsilon_0$, and residue field $K$.

source.place: Propositions 11.1–11.3, printed pp.209–210; direct componentwise expansion over an algebraically closed field

proof.text: To restrict multiplication to $C$, first check that $C\times_K C$ has one point. By Steps 1 and 2, $I=\ker\epsilon$ is the only prime ideal of $B$, and $B=K\cdot1+I$ since $b=\epsilon(b)\cdot1+(b-\epsilon(b)\cdot1)$. Put $D=B\otimes_KB$ and let $J\subseteq D$ be the ideal generated by $I\otimes1$ and $1\otimes I$. Writing $b=\epsilon(b)+i$, $b'=\epsilon(b')+i'$ gives $b\otimes b'\equiv\epsilon(b)\epsilon(b')(1\otimes1)$ modulo $J$, so $D=K(1\otimes1)+J$. Let $P$ be a prime of $D$. Its inverse images under the ring maps $b\mapsto b\otimes1$ and $b\mapsto1\otimes b$ are primes of $B$, hence equal $I$; so $J\subseteq P$. If $\lambda(1\otimes1)+j\in P$ with $\lambda\in K$, $j\in J$, then $\lambda(1\otimes1)\in P$, so $\lambda=0$ because nonzero scalars are units and $P$ is proper. Hence $P=J$: $\operatorname{Spec}D$ has at most one point. By [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-product-affine-spectra] this spectrum is $C\times_K C$, and its point is the image of $(0,0)$. Multiplication sends it to $0$, so factors through the open $C$. Inversion likewise sends the sole point of $C$ to $0$ and factors through $C$; the identity does too. Factorization through an open is restriction of the structure-sheaf maps. The group identities restrict, since open inclusions are monomorphisms. Consequently $C$ is a finite connected commutative subgroup scheme.

source.place: Propositions 11.1–11.3, printed pp.209–210; direct componentwise expansion over an algebraically closed field

proof.text: For $h\in H$, translation $t_h(g)=g+h$ is a scheme automorphism, inverse $t_{-h}$, by the group identities [def-sc-group-scheme]. It sends $0$ to $h$, hence restricts to an isomorphism $C\simeq U_h$ of open subschemes. Define $H_K$ as in [def-weil-pbc-constant-group-scheme]. Its componentwise addition, inverse $h\mapsto-h$, and identity satisfy the group diagrams: on each component they are the corresponding identities in $H$. By [lem-weil-pbc-scheme-coproduct-family], component morphisms glue uniquely. The open subsets of $C\times_K H_K$ pulled back from the components of $H_K$ are disjoint and cover, and each is canonically $C\times_K\operatorname{Spec}K=C$ by the fibre-product universal property [def-pc-fibre-product]. Using [lem-weil-pbc-scheme-morphism-gluing], glue $t_h|_C$ to a map $\phi:C\times_K H_K\to G$. Glue the maps $U_h\to C\times_K H_K$ given by $t_{-h}|_{U_h}$ in the first factor and the constant index $h$ in the second to a map $\psi$. On every open component the two composites are the identity. Thus $\phi$ is a scheme isomorphism with inverse $\psi$.

source.place: Propositions 11.1–11.3, printed pp.209–210; direct componentwise expansion over an algebraically closed field

proof.text: Check the homomorphism equation on the disjoint open cover indexed by $(h,h')\in H^2$ of $(C\times_K H_K)\times_K(C\times_K H_K)$. On this open, for points over every test scheme, the two composites are respectively $(c+c')+(h+h')$ and $(c+h)+(c'+h')$. Associativity and commutativity of $G$ identify them; the first expression uses precisely the restricted law on $C$ from Step 3 and the component law on $H_K$. These are identities of morphisms, since they hold functorially on every test scheme, as in [def-sc-group-scheme]. The identity goes to $0+0=0$ and inversion agrees as well. By [lem-weil-pbc-scheme-morphism-gluing], equality can be checked on the open cover, so $\phi$ is a group-scheme homomorphism. Its inverse is a homomorphism by composing this equation with $\phi^{-1}$ on all factors. This proves the asserted group-scheme isomorphism.

source.place: Propositions 11.1–11.3, printed pp.209–210; direct componentwise expansion over an algebraically closed field

proof.text: The identity point shows $H$ is nonempty, hence $q=|H|\ge1$. The $K$-algebra $B$ is nonzero and contains $K$ injectively (the identity evaluation retracts its scalar map), so $d=\dim_K B\ge1$. Step 4 identifies every $B_h$ with $B$. In the finite product $A\simeq\prod_{h\in H}B_h$ from Step 1, place a basis of each $B_h$ in its coordinate and zero in the other coordinates. These $dq$ vectors span and are independent, coordinate by coordinate. Therefore $\dim_K\Gamma(G,\mathcal O_G)=dq$, completing all clauses.
